title: Unit 2 quiz: Getting Started with Git

options: Creates a hidden .git folder so Git starts tracking this folder
Deletes the history of the project
questions.explain: git init creates the repository (the .git folder) in the current folder. Nothing is uploaded; it is purely local.

questions.q: Put the three stages of Git in the order a change travels.
questions.explain: You edit in the working directory, git add moves changes to the staging area, git commit saves them in the repository.

questions.q: In a new repository, Krish creates menu.txt and runs git status. Under which heading is menu.txt listed?
options: nothing to commit, working tree clean
questions.explain: Git sees the new file but has never saved it, so it is untracked until you git add it.

questions.q: Which command stages every change in the current folder and its subfolders?
questions.explain: git add . stages new, modified and deleted files under the current folder. git commit -a only stages files Git already tracks.

questions.q: You staged secrets.txt by mistake. How do you unstage it but keep the file as it is?
questions.explain: git restore --staged moves the file out of the staging area. Your edits stay. git rm would delete the file.

questions.q: Which is the best commit message?
questions.explain: Good messages say what the commit does and start with a verb, so the history reads like a story.

questions.q: What does the 'M' in the left column of git status -s mean here?
options: menu.txt is modified but not staged
questions.explain: In short status the left column is the staging area and the right column the working directory. M in the left column = staged change. ?? = untracked.

questions.q: What does the -u in git push -u origin main do?
options: Sets origin/main as the upstream, so later plain git push and git pull work
questions.explain: -u (--set-upstream) links your local main to origin/main. Git prints: branch 'main' set up to track 'origin/main'.

questions.q: What is the difference between git fetch and git pull?
options: fetch downloads new commits without changing your branch; pull downloads and merges them
pull only works on the first day
questions.explain: git pull = git fetch + git merge. fetch lets you look first (for example with git log main..origin/main).

questions.q: After git clone https://github.com/hetvi-desai/canteen-docs.git, what is true? (Choose all that apply.)
options: A folder named canteen-docs is created
It contains the full history, not just the files
A remote called origin is already set
You must run git init inside it before committing
questions.explain: clone creates the folder, downloads all history and sets up origin. It is already a repository, so no git init is needed.

questions.q: Your push is rejected with '(fetch first)'. What should you do?
options: Delete the GitHub repository and push again
Run git pull, then git push again
questions.explain: A teammate pushed first. Pull their work (and resolve any conflict), then push. Forcing would overwrite their commits.

questions.q: Put a normal day of teamwork in order.
questions.explain: Start by getting your team's latest work, then edit, check, stage, commit and share.
